questions.prompt: A 10 kg crate is pulled with 30 N on a floor with mu_s = 0.5. It does not move. Which statement is correct?

remediationRefs.label: Review: Static friction is a reaction

options: Friction is 49.05 N, equal to mu_s times the normal force
Friction is 30 N and the crate is below breakaway
Friction is 0 N because the crate has no velocity
The crate must be sliding slowly at constant speed
questions.explanation: mu_s N = 49.05 N exceeds 30 N, so friction equals the applied 30 N.

questions.prompt: A foot with mu_s = 0.9 stands on a ramp. At what angle (degrees, one decimal) does it begin to slip?
A 40 kg robot on a 15 degree ramp has mu_s = 0.2, mu_k = 0.15 (wet). Down-slope acceleration in m/s^2 (two decimals, g = 9.81)?
questions.explanation: tan 15 = 0.268 > 0.2: slides, a = g(sin - mu_k cos) = 1.12.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg mass lands on the floor at 1 m/s (gap 0, v = -1). With h = 0.01 s, what contact force in N does the complementarity step give (one decimal)?
In a time-stepped contact solve, a mass is 0.1 m above the floor and moving up. What is the normal force?
options: mg, because the mass must always be supported
Zero, because the free next gap is positive
Large and positive, to stop the upward motion
Negative, so the floor pulls the mass back down
questions.explanation: If the unconstrained next gap is non-negative the complementarity condition forces lambda = 0.

questions.prompt: A box is 0.30 m wide and 5 kg, pushed at 0.20 m height. Tipping force in N (two decimals, g = 9.81)?
A 5 kg box, 0.30 m wide, sits on a floor with mu_s = 0.6, so its slide force is 29.43 N. At which push height in m (two decimals) do sliding and tipping coincide?
A foot force has F_x = 30 N and F_z = 100 N. What is the smallest friction coefficient for which it is admissible?
A grasp planner approximates a friction cone by a polyhedron inscribed inside the cone. What is the consequence?
options: It overestimates the available friction, so grasps may slip
It has no effect, because the polyhedron and the cone match exactly
It slightly underestimates the capacity, which is conservative
It makes the friction coefficient negative, so forces flip direction
questions.explanation: An inscribed polyhedron lies inside the cone so forces it accepts are truly admissible.

questions.prompt: A block slides at v0 = 3 m/s on a surface with mu_k = 0.3. Stopping distance in m (two decimals, g = 9.81)?
Explicit Euler friction a = -mu g sign(v) with h = 0.01 and mu g h = 0.0245. A block has v = 0.01. Next velocity?
options: 0.01, with no change at all
-0.0345, then it keeps going
-0.0145, then it oscillates
0, the block sticks at once
questions.explanation: The step overshoots zero: 0.01 - 0.0245 = -0.0145, then flips back.

questions.prompt: A robot's wheel slips on a wet ramp that it held when dry. Explain with the friction model what changed and what measurement and design margin you would use.
rubric: Compares required friction ratio |f_t|/N with the available mu_s (tan theta vs mu_s).
Notes wet mu is lower and kinetic friction then applies once slipping starts.
Proposes measuring mu on the real surface and keeping a safety margin.

questions.prompt: Why can a rigid-contact model with four feet on a table give non-unique contact forces and how is a unique answer chosen in practice?
rubric: States statically indeterminate force distribution for rigid bodies.
Mentions adding compliance or choosing by optimisation (minimum norm or friction margin).
Mentions that complementarity constraints still hold for each foot.

questions.prompt: A uniform ladder leans on a wall. Floor friction mu_f = 0.4 and wall friction mu_w = 0.3. Using tan(theta_min) = (1 - mu_f*mu_w)/(2*mu_f) from force and moment balance with both friction cones, what is the smallest angle with the floor (degrees, two decimals) at which it can stand?
questions.explanation: Unknowns f1, N1, N2, f2 with 3 balance equations (f1 = N2, N1 + f2 = mg, N2 tan(theta) + f2 = mg/2). Cone conditions f1 <= mu_f N1 and |f2| <= mu_w N2 are compatible iff 1 <= mu_f (2 tan(theta) + mu_w). So tan(theta) = (1 - 0.12)/0.8 = 1.1 and theta = arctan(1.1) = 47.73 degrees. A frictionless wall would need 51.34 degrees, so wall friction helps.

remediationRefs.label: Review: Equilibrium with two friction cones

questions.prompt: A grasp planner replaces the circular friction cone with an inscribed regular pyramid of k = 8 edges. In the worst tangential direction, what fraction of the true available friction does it still allow?
options: 1/cos(pi/8), about 1.082 (it overestimates)
8 edges give exactly one eighth, 0.125
cos(pi/8), about 0.924
cos(pi/4), about 0.707
questions.explanation: The inscribed polygon has its vertices on the circle of radius mu f_n. Halfway between two vertices the edge is at distance mu f_n cos(pi/k) from the centre, so the worst-case fraction is cos(pi/8) = 0.924. 1/cos(pi/8) is the overshoot of a circumscribed polygon, and cos(pi/4) = 0.707 is the k = 4 value of MR Figure 12.18(c).

questions.prompt: A 2 kg horizontal rod (length 1 m, centre of mass at 0.5 m) rests on one frictional support under x = 0.2 m. A second frictionless support is added. Which placement can balance gravity with both normal forces non-negative?
options: From below at x = 0.35 m, between the first support and the centre of mass
From above at x = 0.0 m, on the far side of the first support
From above at x = 0.8 m, beyond the centre of mass
From below at x = 0.0 m, on the far side of the first support
questions.explanation: Moments about x = 0.2: a contact at b with sign s (+1 from below, -1 from above) needs N2 = mg(0.3)/(s(b-0.2)) >= 0 and N1 = mg - s N2 >= 0. From above, b must be < 0.2, and then N1 = mg + N2 > 0: x = 0.0 gives N2 = 29.43 N, N1 = 49.05 N. From below you need b >= 0.5 (x = 0.35 gives N1 = -19.62 N, a pull; x = 0.0 gives N2 < 0). From above at 0.8 gives N2 < 0.

remediationRefs.label: Review: Unilateral supports and sign conditions
